name: Jade Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the biscuit factory by the canal, on line four, running a flow-wrapper. That's the machine that wraps the packs of biscuits in film and seals the ends. I load the film reels, set the date code, watch for bad seals and clear jams, which happen a lot when the chocolate ones come through a bit warm. The whole building smells like sugar, which you stop noticing after a week, but my clothes never stop smelling of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on line four?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a school dinner lady for twelve years, and when my youngest started school I needed more hours and better money, so a friend got me in here a year and a half ago. I'm still the slow one on changeovers, the supervisor, Grace, has to check my settings. My partner Tomas drives a delivery van, our daughter Elena is fourteen and Benji is eight, and between the mortgage and the van payments there's maybe two weeks of money in the account at the best of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be nice, honestly. Most of what I've seen AI do is write my daughter's homework badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never believed the hype anyway. At work we'd joke about it at break, like "the robot's not coming for your job, Pat, you can stop practising your resignation speech". Online I'd probably share something funny about it and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep learning my job in peace. That's actually what I want: a couple of years to get good at the wrapper and maybe move up to setter. If nothing radical happens, that's my plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Get Grace to teach me changeovers properly so she stops checking me. Maybe use the chatbot now and then like I do now, for letters to the school or the council. Try to save a little, but we always say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Like a normal week, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the chatbot for letters. What was the last one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A letter to the council about the bus to the industrial estate, because they cut the early one and half of us were late every Monday. Elena showed me how. It made it sound much more polite than I would have, which was probably good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And did the bus come back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. But the union rep, Dev, said he'd take it up too. So maybe it'll be the union and not the letter that does it.

S0.say: I never believed the hype anyway, and nobody needs to practise a resignation speech yet. I'd share something funny about it online and leave it at that.
S0.think: A boring AI future means I get to learn my job in peace. That's what I actually want: a couple of years to get good at the wrapper and maybe move up to setter.
S0.do: Carries on and asks the supervisor to teach her changeovers properly. Keeps using the chatbot now and then for letters, and tries to save a little.
S0.quote: It made it sound much more polite than I would have, which was probably good.
S0.fieldNote: Jade sees the slow scenario as permission to keep building her skills at her own pace. She already uses AI tools casually and without much feeling either way. Her story about the bus shows she trusts collective routes like the union alongside her own small efforts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That sounds like what's coming, if I'm honest. They've been talking about a new robot packer for line two for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need to be part of the decision, and the union should be negotiating training for everyone, not just the young lads. I'd say it in the WhatsApp group and at the union meeting. If the government's going to let companies do this, it should help pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I think it means I'm a bit behind again. I've only just started to understand this machine and they'll swap it for one with a screen and a camera. But I'm not scared of a screen, I'll learn it once someone shows me, I learned the till at the school, I learned this. I just don't want to be the one at the back of the queue for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down first for any training they offer, and I'd ask Dev to push for it to be paid. I'd ask Grace if I can shadow the guy who does the robot packer on line two, on my break if I have to. I'd use the chatbot to explain the manuals, because they're written in that awful engineering language. And we'd go through the bills, because Tomas's job might change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous. But a kind of nervous I know, like starting the factory in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas's job might change too. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His company is already using an app that plans the routes, and he says it's decent. But they talk about vans that drive themselves. If both of us are on the list, that's the scary part, not my job on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, who's been on the line twenty-two years and can't read well. She hides it, but she gets me to read out the new safety notices. If everything goes on screens, she's in trouble, and she's too proud to ask.

S1.say: Workers need a say, and the union should be negotiating training for everyone, not just the young lads. Government should help pay for retraining if it lets companies do this.
S1.think: I'm a bit behind again, just when I've learned this machine. I'm not scared of a screen and I'll learn it once someone shows me; I just don't want to be at the back of the queue for training.
S1.do: Puts her name down first for training and asks the union rep to push for it to be paid. Shadows the robot packer operator on line two, uses the chatbot to explain the manuals and goes through the household bills with Tomas.
S1.feel: Nervous in a familiar way, like when she first started at the factory.
S1.quote: If both of us are on the list, that's the scary part, not my job on its own.
S1.fieldNote: Jade's worry is about the household, not just her job: Tomas's delivery work is exposed too. She's ready to learn once shown, which fits her steady approach. Her concern for Pat, who hides that she struggles to read, was unprompted and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years. That's… Elena would be sixteen. Benji ten. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong rules and strong unions, and that the government has to step in now with some kind of basic income. I'd sign every petition. I'd tell people it isn't their fault, because a lot of people would blame themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think both of us would lose our jobs inside a year, me and Tomas. A robot that can do anything won't need a slow woman on a flow-wrapper, and it won't need a man driving a van. And we've got two weeks of money. That's what I keep coming back to, two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go to the bank and the council and ask what help there is before we need it, because I've seen people wait too long. We'd cut everything: Benji's swimming, the phones down to the cheapest, no holiday. I'd look for work in care or cleaning, things with people, maybe at Benji's school kitchen again, though who knows if that lasts. I'd join whatever the union organises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. Like that feeling when you realise you've left the kids somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell people it isn't their fault. Would you believe that about yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd think, you should have stayed in school, you should have done a course years ago. But I'd say it to Pat and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first bill that goes unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van loan, probably, because if Tomas has no job the van's no use anyway. Then the credit card. The mortgage last, I'd sell the furniture before I'd miss the mortgage.

S2.say: We need strong rules, strong unions and some kind of basic income from the government now. I'd sign every petition and tell people it isn't their fault.
S2.think: I think Tomas and I would both lose our jobs inside a year, and we've got about two weeks of money. That's what I keep coming back to, two weeks.
S2.do: Goes to the bank and the council in the first month to ask what help exists, and cuts swimming, phone plans and holidays. Looks for care, cleaning or school kitchen work and joins whatever the union organises.
S2.feel: Sick to her stomach, a sharp, sudden fear.
S2.quote: I'd sell the furniture before I'd miss the mortgage.
S2.fieldNote: The double exposure of two low-paid jobs in one house drives her fear here. She'd act early and practically, asking for help before a crisis, which she's seen others fail to do. She'd forgive others but not herself, a gap between her public kindness and private self-blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's not nothing. Benji would be thirteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them: proper funded retraining, rules about how fast companies can replace people, and a safety net that's ready before it lands. I'd go to the union meetings and actually speak, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for me to get into something with people, like care work or teaching assistant, where a robot might come last. It's not enough to make us safe. But it's enough to not be caught standing there like with the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in care, the free one at the college if there is one. I'd use the chatbot to help with the coursework, Elena would laugh at me. We'd try to save the money Tomas gets from overtime instead of spending it. And I'd keep going to the union, because it's the only thing that makes the company listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have something to do with it. Doing something helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work might be where a robot comes last. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen my mum in the home. What she needs is someone to hold her hand and remember she likes her tea weak. Maybe a robot can lift her, fine, but I don't think families would want a robot doing all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the factory, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away, we can't afford a gap. I'd do the course in the evenings and switch when I had a job lined up, maybe year three. I'm not a jump-first person, but I'm not going to stand still either.

S3.say: We have five years, so let's use them: funded retraining, limits on how fast companies replace people, and a safety net ready before it lands. I'd actually speak at union meetings.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to move into work with people, like care, where a robot might come last. It won't make us safe, but at least we won't be caught standing still.
S3.do: Starts a free evening care course at the college in the first year, using the chatbot for coursework, and saves Tomas's overtime money. Plans to switch jobs around year three once something is lined up.
S3.feel: Worried, but steadier because she has something to work on.
S3.quote: What she needs is someone to hold her hand and remember she likes her tea weak.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Jade's fear into a plan, built around her mother's care home. She won't jump without a job lined up, a clear sign of how thin their savings are. Wanting to speak at union meetings for the first time shows the scenario pushing her past her usual quietness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Elena would be twenty-four. That changes things, doesn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is no excuse for anyone being left behind. The government has time to build a proper plan, and the companies have time to train people. I'd be saying that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be okay-ish. I'd have time to do the care training, move over, get some years in. The kids would be grown or nearly. The end point still scares me, but I'd be fifty-three and maybe in a job where people still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care course over two years, slowly, while working. I'd talk to Elena seriously about what she studies, not something a robot will do. We'd try to pay the van off early and save a bit. I'd still use the chatbot, more probably, to learn things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than scared. It's like seeing weather coming from far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elena about her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to do graphic design. I'd tell her, love, the computer can already draw. I'd push her towards nursing or being a physio, something with hands and people. She'd roll her eyes. She'd probably do design anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both of you might be okay-ish. What about Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas says he'll be the last man driving a van, but he says that about everything. In ten years he could learn to fix the electric vans, maybe. I'd have to push him, he's even slower than me with new things.

S4.say: Ten years is no excuse for anyone being left behind. The government has time to build a proper plan and companies have time to train people.
S4.think: I think we'd be okay-ish: time to do the care training and get some years in, with the kids grown. The end point still scares me, but I might be in a job where people still want a person.
S4.do: Takes the care course slowly over two years while working and pushes Elena towards nursing or physiotherapy. Pays off the van early, saves a bit and uses AI tools more to learn.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than scared.
S4.quote: I'd tell her, love, the computer can already draw.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Jade's plan is the same as with five, just calmer, and her attention moves to her kids' futures. She worries more about Tomas adapting than herself. The image of weather seen from far away sums up how distance softens the threat for her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd both go at once and we've got nothing behind us. What would help is an income that kicks in straight away, not after months of forms, and free training you can do in the evenings with childcare covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the women on the line. Most of us came in late, after kids, and we're the ones still learning. When they cut, they cut the newest first, and the newest is us.

headlineQuote: When they cut, they cut the newest first, and the newest is us.
portrait: Jade is a forty-three-year-old flow-wrapper operator at a biscuit factory, eighteen months in after twelve years as a school dinner lady. She leans left, trusts the union, and uses a chatbot now and then for letters and manuals. Her biggest fear is that she and her van-driver partner Tomas lose work at the same time with about two weeks of money behind them. Given time, she'd retrain slowly into care work, inspired by her mother's care home, and steer her daughter towards jobs with people.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Tomas would lose their jobs at the same time with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: An income that starts straight away without months of forms, and free evening training with childcare covered.
